description: How Western (and some non-Western) music works and how it changed: what you can hear that marks each era from chant to techno, what each innovation solved, and a few canonical works as anchors.

notes.front: Physically, what is pitch and what is loudness?
notes.back: Pitch = frequency of vibration (Hz, how fast); loudness = amplitude (how big the pressure swing).
notes.extra: Reference: A4 = 440 Hz is modern concert pitch; Baroque ensembles often use 415 Hz, a semitone lower.

notes.front: Why does a note an octave higher sound like 'the same note'?
notes.back: Its frequency is exactly double (2:1), so every harmonic of the upper note coincides with one of the lower: maximal fusion.
notes.analogy: The same colour, one shade lighter: different, yet obviously the same hue.

notes.front: What is the overtone (harmonic) series?
notes.back: A vibrating string or air column sounds its fundamental f plus integer multiples 2f, 3f, 4f… The mix of their strengths is the timbre.
notes.analogy: A skipping rope can wave in one big arc or in two, three, four smaller loops; a string does all of these at once.
notes.extra: Hear it: Bugle calls and natural horns can only play notes of this series; brass players 'lip' between them.

notes.text: Reading up the harmonic series, the intervals shrink: octave (2:1), then the {{c1::perfect fifth}} (3:2), the {{c2::perfect fourth}} (4:3), the {{c3::major third}} (5:4), and the flat 'blue' 7th harmonic.

notes.front: Why do the octave and perfect fifth sound consonant while a minor second sounds harsh?
notes.back: Simple ratios (2:1, 3:2) make the two notes' harmonics largely coincide; complex ratios make nearby partials beat against each other (roughness).
notes.analogy: Two gears mesh smoothly when their teeth line up often (simple ratio) and grind when they rarely do.
notes.extra: Nuance: What counts as 'dissonant' is also learned: thirds were dissonant to medieval ears and tritones were avoided for centuries.

notes.front: How is an interval named?
notes.back: By letter-step count (second, third… octave) plus quality: perfect (unison, 4th, 5th, 8ve), major/minor, or augmented/diminished.
notes.extra: Example: C–E = major third (4 semitones); C–E♭ = minor third (3); C–F♯ = augmented fourth (the tritone).

notes.text: The major scale's step pattern is W–W–H–W–W–W–H: the half steps fall between degrees {{c1::3–4}} and {{c2::7–8}}; the 7th degree is the {{c3::leading tone}} pulling up to the tonic.

notes.front: Scale vs mode: what is the difference?
notes.back: A scale is an ordered set of pitches. A mode is that set heard with a particular note as home: rotate the white keys and C-Ionian becomes D-Dorian, with a different colour.
notes.analogy: Same seven ingredients, different dish depending on which one you build the plate around.

notes.front: How do you hear major vs minor?
notes.back: Listen for the third above the tonic: a major third (4 semitones) sounds bright and open; a minor third (3 semitones) sounds darker.
notes.extra: Pitfall: 'Sad' and 'happy' are cultural shorthand: fast minor can be fiery (flamenco), slow major can be melancholy.

notes.text: The church modes on the white keys, in order from C: Ionian, {{c1::Dorian}} (D, minor with raised 6th: 'Scarborough Fair'), {{c2::Phrygian}} (E, flat 2nd: Spanish/flamenco colour), Lydian (F), {{c3::Mixolydian}} (G, major with flat 7th: much rock), Aeolian (A, natural minor), Locrian (B).

notes.front: Why does the pentatonic scale turn up in so many cultures and sound so 'safe'?
notes.back: Five notes with no semitones between any pair, so nothing clashes; found in Chinese, Celtic, Javanese and African-American music (and the black piano keys).
notes.extra: Hear it: 'Amazing Grace', 'Auld Lang Syne', most blues-rock guitar solos.

notes.front: What is tonality (a key)?
notes.back: Organising pitches around a tonic: one home note and chord to which the others gravitate, creating tension when you leave and release when you return.
notes.analogy: Gravity: every chord has a felt weight and distance from the ground floor.

notes.front: What is a triad, and what decides whether it is major or minor?
notes.back: Three notes stacked in thirds: root, third, fifth. A major third at the bottom gives a major triad; a minor third gives minor.
notes.extra: Also: diminished (two minor thirds: tense) and augmented (two major thirds: floating).

notes.front: In tonal harmony, what jobs do the tonic, subdominant and dominant do?
notes.back: Tonic (I): home and rest. Subdominant (IV): departure, preparation. Dominant (V): tension that demands a return to I.
notes.analogy: Home, the road out, and the moment at the door with your key in the lock.

notes.front: Why does the dominant chord 'want' to resolve to the tonic?
notes.back: It contains the leading tone, a semitone below the tonic; as a V7 it also holds a tritone whose two notes resolve by step into the tonic chord.

notes.text: Cadences: V→I is a {{c1::perfect (authentic)}} cadence, a full stop; IV→I is {{c2::plagal}} (the 'Amen'); a phrase ending on V is a {{c3::half cadence}}, a comma; V→vi instead of I is {{c4::deceptive (interrupted)}}.

notes.front: Why does a Classical 4+4-bar phrase pair usually end its first half on a half cadence and its second on a perfect cadence?
notes.back: The first phrase asks a question (comma, ending on V, unresolved); the second answers it (full stop, V→I). The balanced pairing of tension and resolution is the Classical phrase.

notes.front: What is the circle of fifths, and what does distance on it tell you?
notes.back: All 12 keys arranged so neighbours are a fifth apart and differ by one sharp/flat. Close keys share almost all notes (smooth modulation); distant keys sound like a jolt.
notes.analogy: A colour wheel: neighbours blend, opposites clash.
notes.extra: Use: Sonata form moves to the neighbour (V); Romantic composers leap to distant thirds for drama.

notes.front: What is modulation, and why does it matter for large-scale form?
notes.back: Changing key during a piece. Leaving home creates tension over minutes, not seconds; returning gives large-scale resolution. Classical forms are built on it.
notes.analogy: A scene change in a play: the longer you are away from the hero's home, the stronger the homecoming.

notes.front: Beat vs metre vs rhythm?
notes.back: Beat: the steady pulse. Metre: how beats group into recurring strong–weak patterns (bars of 3, 4…). Rhythm: the actual note durations played against that grid.
notes.analogy: Metre is the ruled lines on graph paper, the beat their spacing, rhythm the curve you draw on them.

notes.front: 6/8 and 3/4 both hold six quavers per bar. How do they sound different?
notes.back: 6/8 is two beats each split in three (ONE-and-a TWO-and-a, a lilt); 3/4 is three beats each split in two (ONE-two-three, a waltz).
notes.extra: Hear it: Bernstein's 'America' alternates the two bar by bar: 'I like to be in A-me-ri-ca' (6/8 then 3/4).

notes.front: What is syncopation?
notes.back: Accents placed off the expected strong beats or between beats; you hear the grid and the push against it at once.
notes.extra: Hear it: Ragtime, jazz, funk, reggae. Without a felt grid there is no syncopation, only irregularity.

notes.front: A flute and an oboe play the same pitch. What makes them sound different (timbre)?
notes.back: Different overtone mixes (oboe: rich, nasal; flute: nearly pure) plus the attack envelope. The brain leans heavily on the first few milliseconds.
notes.analogy: Two people saying the same word on the same pitch: you still know instantly who is speaking.
notes.extra: Experiment: Cut the attack off a recording and a piano, guitar and harp become hard to tell apart.

notes.text: Textures: a single unaccompanied line is {{c1::monophony}} (chant); a melody over chordal accompaniment is {{c2::homophony}} (hymn, most pop); several independent melodies at once is {{c3::polyphony}} (fugue).

notes.front: What is counterpoint?
notes.back: The craft of combining independent melodic lines so each sings on its own and together they make coherent harmony; governed by rules on consonance and motion.
notes.analogy: A good conversation: everyone speaks their own sentence, yet nobody talks over the point.

notes.text: Small forms: AB is {{c1::binary}}; ABA is {{c2::ternary}}; ABACADA is {{c3::rondo}} (a refrain returning between episodes); a theme restated and altered each time is {{c4::variation form}}.

notes.front: Why does music tolerate (and need) far more repetition than speech?
notes.back: Repetition is what makes structure audible: a phrase heard again is recognised as a unit, and expectation can be set up, delayed and satisfied.
notes.extra: Evidence: Loop a spoken phrase and it starts to sound sung (Diana Deutsch's speech-to-song illusion).

notes.text: The orchestra's four sections: {{c1::strings}} (violins, violas, cellos, basses), {{c2::woodwind}} (flutes, oboes, clarinets, bassoons), {{c3::brass}} (horns, trumpets, trombones, tuba) and {{c4::percussion}}.

notes.front: Why are the strings the core of the orchestra rather than winds?
notes.back: They blend into one homogeneous tone across the whole range, sustain indefinitely, play very softly or loudly and move fast; winds and brass add colour on top.
notes.extra: Numbers: Roughly 60 of a 100-player orchestra are strings.

notes.front: How do you tell flute, oboe and clarinet apart by ear?
notes.back: Flute: pure, breathy, few overtones. Oboe: nasal, reedy, penetrating. Clarinet: hollow, 'woody' low register (odd harmonics only), huge range and dynamic span.
notes.extra: Why the oboe gives the tuning A: its pitch is stable and hard to bend, and its tone cuts through.

notes.front: Compare Haydn's and Mahler's orchestras: what changes in size and instrumentation, and what do you hear as a result?
notes.back: Haydn: ~35 players, pairs of winds, horns and trumpets, no trombones. Mahler: 100+, triple or quadruple winds, 8 horns, harps, celesta. Hear it as dynamic range and colour variety.

notes.front: Why did the valve (c. 1815) transform brass writing?
notes.back: Natural horns and trumpets could only play one harmonic series per crook; valves add tubing instantly, giving a full chromatic scale. Brass turned from fanfare to melody (Wagner, Bruckner).
notes.extra: Hear it: Beethoven's horns sit on open notes and leap; Wagner's horns sing long chromatic lines.

notes.front: Harpsichord vs piano: what mechanical difference explains the sound?
notes.back: Harpsichord plucks the string with a quill: fixed loudness, no touch dynamics. Piano strikes with a felt hammer: louder when struck harder, hence 'pianoforte'.
notes.analogy: A light switch versus a dimmer.

notes.front: What problem did Cristofori's piano action (c. 1700) solve?
notes.back: A keyboard that plays soft and loud by touch: the escapement lets the hammer strike and fall back freely instead of staying pressed against the string.

notes.front: Why does a modern grand sound so much bigger than Mozart's fortepiano?
notes.back: The cast-iron frame (1820s on) takes enormous string tension; thicker strings, cross-stringing and felt hammers give power and long sustain. Mozart's instrument is lighter, quicker to decay, more speech-like.
notes.extra: Consequence: Chopin's and Liszt's writing presupposes the new sustain and volume.

notes.front: Why did the electric guitar matter for the birth of rock?
notes.back: Amplification let one guitar match drums and horns in volume; pushing the amp into overdrive added sustain and harmonic richness, a new timbre no acoustic instrument had.

notes.front: What did the phonograph (1877) and the pressed disc (Berliner, 1890s) change in principle?
notes.back: Performance was separated from presence: music became a repeatable object you could own. Mass-pressable discs created the record industry.
notes.analogy: Photography for sound: a passing moment becomes an object you can carry home.
notes.extra: Side effect: Styles that didn't fit on a disc side, or didn't record well (soft strings vs loud brass), were shaped by the medium.

notes.front: Why are pop songs about three minutes long?
notes.back: A 10-inch 78 rpm disc side held roughly three minutes; radio and jukebox formats then preserved the habit long after the constraint vanished.

notes.front: What did the microphone and electrical recording (1925) do to singing?
notes.back: A quiet, intimate voice could now fill a record and a hall. Crooning (Bing Crosby) replaced operatic projection as the pop ideal.

notes.front: What did magnetic tape (post-1945) make possible?
notes.back: Editing by cutting and splicing, overdubbing, speed and direction changes. The studio became an instrument (Les Paul; musique concrète; the Beatles' Sgt. Pepper).
notes.analogy: Cut-and-paste arrives for sound, decades before the word processor.

notes.front: Why is multitrack recording a change in how music is composed, not just recorded?
notes.back: Parts are recorded separately and layered, so the performance never has to happen all at once; the producer assembles the piece after the fact.
notes.analogy: From live theatre to film editing.

notes.front: In one breath: how does a subtractive synthesiser make a sound?
notes.back: An oscillator makes a harmonically rich wave (saw, square); a filter carves away harmonics; an envelope shapes loudness over time; an amplifier outputs it.

notes.text: ADSR envelope: {{c1::attack}} is the time to reach peak, {{c2::decay}} the fall to the held level, {{c3::sustain}} that level while the key is down, {{c4::release}} the fade after key-up.
notes.extra: Hear it: A plucked sound is fast attack + fast decay; a pad is slow attack + long release.

notes.front: Moog (1960s) vs Yamaha DX7 (1983): what is the difference in sound and method?
notes.back: Moog: analogue voltage-controlled subtractive synthesis, warm and fat, originally monophonic. DX7: digital FM synthesis, glassy electric pianos, bells and basses that defined 1980s pop.
notes.extra: Lineage: FM synthesis was invented by John Chowning at Stanford (1967–73) and licensed to Yamaha.

notes.front: What is sampling, and what did it change about what counts as an instrument?
notes.back: Recording a real sound and replaying it at any pitch or on a trigger pad. Any sound, including other records, became playable material (Fairlight, Akai MPC, hip-hop).
notes.analogy: Collage: cutting pictures out of magazines to make a new picture.

notes.front: What is MIDI (1983), and why does it matter that it carries no audio?
notes.back: A standard for note and controller messages between instruments and computers. Separating the score data from the sound made sequencing, editing and the DAW possible.
notes.analogy: MIDI is the sheet music; the synthesiser is the player. Swap the player and the same file sounds different.

notes.front: How have formats kept shaping song and album length?
notes.back: 78 side → 3-minute song; LP (c. 20 min a side) → the album as an artistic unit; CD (74 min) → bloated albums; streaming → shorter tracks with the hook in the first 30 seconds (royalty threshold).

notes.front: What did the Pythagoreans discover about consonance, and why did it matter for 2,000 years?
notes.back: Consonant intervals correspond to simple string-length ratios: 2:1 octave, 3:2 fifth, 4:3 fourth. Music became audible number, a branch of mathematics ('harmony of the spheres').
notes.extra: Legacy: Via Boethius, music sat in the medieval quadrivium with arithmetic, geometry and astronomy, so theory stayed mathematical and prestigious.

notes.front: How is Pythagorean tuning built, and what is its flaw?
notes.back: Stack pure 3:2 fifths. But twelve fifths overshoot seven octaves by the Pythagorean comma (~24 cents), so one 'wolf' fifth is sour and major thirds (81:64) are harsh.
notes.analogy: Tiling a floor with slightly-too-big tiles: eleven fit, the twelfth has to be forced.

notes.front: Why can no keyboard tuning have pure fifths, pure thirds and every key usable? How did Pythagorean, meantone and equal tunings each compromise?
notes.back: Stacked pure fifths overshoot the octave, so something must give. Pythagorean: pure fifths, harsh thirds, one wolf fifth. Meantone: narrowed fifths, pure thirds, remote keys unusable. Equal: every key usable, nothing pure except octaves.

notes.front: Why did medieval theory call thirds dissonant while the Renaissance built everything on them?
notes.back: In Pythagorean tuning the third is rough (81:64). Once tuning shifted toward pure 5:4 thirds (meantone, 15th c.), triads sounded sweet and became the basic sound.
notes.extra: Hear it: English 15th-century music (Dunstaple) sounded strikingly 'sweet' to continental ears: the contenance angloise.

notes.front: What can you hear that says 'Gregorian chant'?
notes.back: A single unaccompanied line in Latin, free unmetred rhythm following the text, modal (not major/minor), mostly stepwise, sung by men in a resonant church.

notes.front: Syllabic vs melismatic chant?
notes.back: Syllabic: one note per syllable (psalm tones, hymns). Melismatic: many notes on one syllable (the long 'Alleluia' flourish), expressing jubilation beyond words.

notes.front: What problem was neume notation (9th century) solving?
notes.back: Charlemagne's court wanted one uniform Roman liturgy across the empire, and singers had thousands of chants to remember. Neumes fixed the melodic shape as a memory aid.

notes.front: What did Guido of Arezzo (c. 1030) add to notation, and what did it enable?
notes.back: Staff lines with clefs fixing exact pitch, plus the syllables ut–re–mi–fa–sol–la for sight-singing. A singer could now learn a chant from the page without a teacher.
notes.extra: Claim: Guido said his method cut training from ten years to one.

notes.front: Why was exact pitch notation a revolution rather than a convenience?
notes.back: It made composition a written, planned act and let several coordinated voices be designed in advance. Music became a 'work' separable from any performance.
notes.analogy: Like moving from oral storytelling to the written novel: longer, more intricate structures become possible.

notes.front: What is organum?
notes.back: The earliest written polyphony (9th–12th c.): a second voice added to a chant, first in parallel fourths or fifths, later moving freely, then florid runs over long held chant notes.
notes.analogy: A shadow that first follows the chant at a fixed distance, then learns to walk on its own.
notes.extra: Hear it: Open, hollow fifths and octaves; the chant stretched into a slow drone underneath.

notes.front: What did the Notre Dame school (Léonin, Pérotin, c. 1200) invent?
notes.back: Rhythmic notation: the rhythmic modes (fixed long–short patterns) let several voices coordinate precisely. Pérotin wrote the first four-voice pieces.

notes.front: What did mensural notation (Franco of Cologne, c. 1280) add?
notes.back: Note shape now meant duration (long, breve, semibreve), freeing rhythm from the fixed rhythmic modes. The ancestor of our note values.

notes.front: Ars Nova (14th century, Vitry, Machaut): what changed in how rhythm was written and used?
notes.back: Duple metre was admitted as equal to the 'perfect' triple, and smaller note values appeared. Rhythm became a compositional playground (isorhythm, sophisticated secular polyphonic songs).
notes.extra: Anchor: Machaut's Messe de Nostre Dame, the first complete polyphonic Mass by one composer.

notes.front: What is isorhythm?
notes.back: A repeating rhythmic pattern (talea) combined with a repeating melodic pattern (color) of a different length in the tenor, so they realign only after many cycles: hidden architecture.
notes.analogy: Two gears with different tooth counts: the same tooth pair meets again only after many turns.

notes.front: What did the troubadours and trouvères contribute (12th–13th c.)?
notes.back: Secular song in the vernacular on courtly love, by named poet-composers outside the church. Song became an art with authors.

notes.front: Medieval vs Renaissance polyphony: how to tell them apart by ear?
notes.back: Medieval: angular lines, hollow fifths and octaves at cadences, voices with different rhythms or even texts, a tenor drone. Renaissance: smooth imitation, full triads, blended equal voices.

notes.front: What is a cantus firmus?
notes.back: A pre-existing melody (a chant or a song like L'homme armé) used as the structural backbone of a polyphonic piece, usually in long notes in the tenor.
notes.analogy: The steel frame of a building: hidden, load-bearing, everything else hung on it.
notes.extra: Scale: Over 40 Renaissance Masses were built on L'homme armé: a shared benchmark for compositional skill.

notes.front: What can you hear that says 'Renaissance'?
notes.back: Smooth a cappella polyphony, voices entering in imitation, full consonant triads, equal voices with no soloist, text-driven phrasing, a calm 'oceanic' flow.

notes.front: What is imitative polyphony, and how do you recognise it?
notes.back: Each voice enters in turn with the same motif, like a round, then goes its own way. Listen for a tune starting again in another voice a few beats later.
notes.analogy: A round like 'Frère Jacques', except the voices are then allowed to wander off and develop.
notes.extra: Lineage: The ancestor of the Baroque fugue.

notes.front: Why is Josquin des Prez the anchor of the high Renaissance?
notes.back: He perfected imitation and made music follow the meaning of the text; the first composer whose name sold prints. Anchor: Ave Maria… virgo serena.
notes.extra: Luther: 'Josquin is master of the notes; others are mastered by them.'

notes.front: What did music printing (Petrucci, Venice 1501) change?
notes.back: Repertoire spread beyond the chapel that commissioned it, and amateurs bought partbooks. Composers became famous across Europe and notation standardised.
notes.analogy: From manuscripts copied for one chapel to a catalogue anyone in Europe can order from.

notes.front: Mass vs motet vs madrigal?
notes.back: Mass: the five fixed Latin Ordinary texts. Motet: sacred polyphony on any other Latin text. Madrigal: secular vernacular poetry, intimate, full of word-painting.

notes.text: The Ordinary of the Mass, set by composers from Machaut to Stravinsky: Kyrie, {{c1::Gloria}}, {{c2::Credo}}, Sanctus (with Benedictus), {{c3::Agnus Dei}}.

notes.front: What is word-painting (madrigalism)?
notes.back: Music imitating the words' meaning: a rising line on 'ascend', a rest on 'sigh', a dissonance on 'death', two voices on 'together'. The madrigal's whole game.
notes.analogy: Emoji in sound: the music acts out the word as it is sung.
notes.extra: Anchors: Marenzio, Monteverdi's books, Weelkes's As Vesta Was. The road leads straight to opera.

notes.front: What did the Council of Trent want from church music, and how did Palestrina answer?
notes.back: Intelligible words, no secular tunes, dignity. Palestrina's clear declamation and controlled dissonance (Missa Papae Marcelli) became the model, and later the textbook of counterpoint.

notes.front: Why is Palestrina style still taught as 'species counterpoint'?
notes.back: Its rules (mostly stepwise, leaps balanced, dissonance only passing or prepared and resolved by step) train clean voice-leading that every later style assumes.
notes.extra: Lineage: Fux's Gradus ad Parnassum (1725) codified it; Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven all studied it.

notes.front: A composer writes two voices moving in parallel fifths. Why does Palestrina-style counterpoint forbid it?
notes.back: Parallel perfect intervals fuse the two voices into one thickened line, destroying their independence. The rules demand contrary or oblique motion so each voice stays a distinct melody.

notes.front: What musical consequence did the Reformation have?
notes.back: Luther wanted the congregation to sing: vernacular hymns (chorales such as Ein feste Burg), later Bach's raw material. Calvinists allowed only unaccompanied psalms.

notes.front: What was the Venetian cori spezzati (split-choir) technique, and what did it lead to?
notes.back: Choirs and instruments placed apart in St Mark's answering each other in space (Gabrieli). The contrast principle grew into the Baroque concerto.
notes.analogy: Stereo before stereo: sound arriving from different corners of the room.

notes.front: What is meantone temperament, and what trade-off did it make?
notes.back: Fifths narrowed slightly so major thirds come out pure (5:4). Gorgeous triads in common keys; remote keys become unusable.
notes.analogy: Optimising for the common case: perfect at home, broken at the edges.
notes.extra: Arc: Pythagorean (pure fifths) → meantone (pure thirds) → well → equal temperament (nothing pure, everything usable).

notes.front: What role did instrumental music play in the Renaissance?
notes.back: Secondary but growing: dance pairs (pavane–galliard), consorts of viols or recorders, lute song. Independent instrumental forms only take off in the Baroque.

notes.front: What can you hear that says 'Baroque'?
notes.back: A continuous driving 'motor' rhythm, a harpsichord filling in chords under a busy bass, one mood per movement, ornamented melody, terraced (stepped) dynamics, small forces.

notes.front: What is basso continuo, and why does it define the era?
notes.back: A bass line with figures (numbers) from which harpsichord, organ or lute improvised the chords. Thinking shifted from equal polyphonic voices to melody over a harmonic bass.
notes.analogy: A jazz chord chart: the bass and the symbols are written, the realisation is the player's.

notes.front: How did basso continuo practice lead to the theory of chords with roots and functions?
notes.back: Players read figured bass and thought in vertical chords above a bass note. Theorists such as Rameau (1722) then described chords as units with roots, giving the functional harmony of tonic, subdominant and dominant.

notes.front: What was monody (seconda pratica), and what did it react against?
notes.back: A solo voice with chordal accompaniment, following speech and emotion. Reaction against Renaissance polyphony, where overlapping voices buried the words: 'the text should be master of the harmony' (Monteverdi).

notes.front: Why was opera born around 1600 in Florence, and what did it try to recreate?
notes.back: Humanist scholars believed Greek drama was sung throughout and moved audiences to tears. Recitative was invented to sing the plot in speech rhythm. Anchor: Monteverdi's Orfeo (1607).

notes.front: Recitative vs aria?
notes.back: Recitative: speech-like, free rhythm, sparse continuo, carries the plot. Aria: lyrical, metrical, orchestral, a frozen moment of one emotion (often da capo ABA).
notes.analogy: Dialogue scene vs musical number: the plot stops so the feeling can be sung.

notes.front: What is the doctrine of the affections, and how does it shape a Baroque movement?
notes.back: Each aria or movement portrays one emotion (affect) steadily from start to end. Contrast is between movements, not within them: the opposite of the Classical style.
notes.analogy: A portrait rather than a film: one expression, held.

notes.front: What is a concerto grosso, and what aesthetic does it embody?
notes.back: A small group of soloists (concertino) alternating with the full ensemble (ripieno). The Baroque love of contrast, light versus shade, made audible. Anchors: Corelli, Bach's Brandenburgs.
notes.analogy: Chiaroscuro painting: the whole effect comes from light set against shade.

notes.front: What is ritornello form?
notes.back: An orchestral refrain returns (in different keys) between solo episodes. Vivaldi's concerto first movements use it; it fathers the Classical rondo and concerto.

notes.front: What did Vivaldi fix in place?
notes.back: The three-movement concerto (fast–slow–fast), ritornello form, and virtuoso solo writing, across ~500 concertos. Bach learned by transcribing them. Anchor: The Four Seasons.

notes.front: What is a fugue?
notes.back: A contrapuntal piece in which a subject is stated alone, then imitated by each voice in turn (exposition), followed by episodes and re-entries in new keys.
notes.analogy: A topic handed round a dinner table: each guest repeats it in turn, then the conversation develops it.
notes.extra: Hear it: Count the entries at the start: that is the number of voices.

notes.text: Fugue vocabulary: the opening theme is the {{c1::subject}}; its restatement in the next voice a fifth away is the {{c2::answer}}; a passage without the main theme is an {{c3::episode}}; entries overlapping before the previous one finishes is {{c4::stretto}}.

notes.front: Why is Bach the anchor of the era, and which works?
notes.back: He fused counterpoint with the new tonal harmony at the highest level: Well-Tempered Clavier, Brandenburg Concertos, St Matthew Passion, Mass in B minor, Goldberg Variations.
notes.extra: Reception: Provincial and old-fashioned in his lifetime; canonised after Mendelssohn's 1829 St Matthew Passion revival.

notes.front: What does 'Well-Tempered' in Bach's title mean, and what was he demonstrating?
notes.back: A keyboard tuned so that all 24 major and minor keys are usable (well temperament, not necessarily equal). The cycle proves the whole circle of keys is now navigable.

notes.front: Equal temperament: what does it solve and what does it cost?
notes.back: Every semitone identical, so any key, modulation and transposition work. Cost: no interval except the octave is pure (major thirds 14 cents sharp), and every key has the same colour.
notes.analogy: A universal travel adapter: fits every socket, perfect in none.
notes.extra: Adoption: Standard on pianos only in the 19th century; string players and singers still bend toward pure intervals.

notes.text: Equal temperament divides the octave into 12 equal semitones of ratio \(2^{1/12} \approx 1.0595\); measured in cents (100 per semitone), its fifth is {{c1::2 cents}} narrow and its major third {{c2::14 cents}} wide compared with pure 3:2 and 5:4.

notes.front: Handel vs Bach: how do they differ?
notes.back: Handel: cosmopolitan, theatrical, bold simple gestures, Italian opera then English oratorio for a paying public (Messiah). Bach: Lutheran church and court, dense counterpoint, instructive, local.

notes.front: Oratorio vs opera?
notes.back: Oratorio: a sacred story in concert, unstaged, with a prominent chorus. Handel invented the English oratorio when Italian opera stopped paying and the Lenten theatre ban bit.

notes.text: The core Baroque dance suite: a moderate German {{c1::allemande}}, a flowing {{c2::courante}}, a slow stately {{c3::sarabande}}, a fast jig-like {{c4::gigue}}; Bach often adds a prelude and optional dances (minuet, bourrée, gavotte) just before the last one.

notes.front: List the four core dances of the Baroque suite in order and describe each one's character.
notes.back: Allemande (moderate, German); courante (flowing); sarabande (slow, stately); gigue (fast, jig-like). Slow-to-fast closure; Bach often inserts a prelude and optional dances.

notes.front: What is a ground bass (chaconne, passacaglia)?
notes.back: A short bass pattern repeating throughout while the upper parts vary above it. Hear the bass loop and the growing intensity on top.
notes.analogy: A loop pedal: the bass repeats while the solo evolves above it.
notes.extra: Anchors: Purcell's Dido's Lament, Bach's Chaconne for violin, Pachelbel's Canon; the same idea as a pop chord loop.

notes.front: How much of a Baroque score is actually written down?
notes.back: A skeleton: performers added trills and ornaments, embellished repeats, realised the continuo and improvised cadenzas. The 'historically informed performance' movement rediscovered this.
notes.analogy: A lead sheet, not a MIDI file: the notation expects you to add.

notes.front: Baroque vs Classical: four quick tells?
notes.back: Dynamics: terraced vs graded crescendos. Texture: polyphony with continuo vs melody and accompaniment. Mood: one affect vs contrasts within a movement. Phrases: spun-out vs balanced 4+4 bars.

notes.front: What can you hear that says 'Classical'?
notes.back: Clear balanced phrases (question–answer, 4+4 bars), melody over light accompaniment, moods contrasting within a movement, gradual crescendos, transparent texture, no harpsichord continuo.

notes.front: What did the Classical style react against in the Baroque?
notes.back: Dense counterpoint and heavy ornament seemed 'learned' and artificial. Enlightenment taste wanted clarity, naturalness and wit (the galant style).

notes.front: Sonata form in one breath?
notes.back: Exposition: theme 1 at home, theme 2 in a new key (dominant or relative major). Development: fragments, modulation, instability. Recapitulation: both themes at home. Coda optional.

notes.front: Why is sonata form really about keys, not tunes?
notes.back: The plot is harmonic: leaving home creates tension, the development is the crisis, and resolution comes when the second theme, first heard away, returns in the home key.
notes.analogy: The themes are the characters; the key is the plot. Same cast, different place, then home.

notes.front: What would go wrong in a sonata form if the second theme returned in the dominant key in the recapitulation?
notes.back: The piece would never resolve: the second theme would still sound 'away from home', so the central conflict is unsettled. Recapitulating both themes in the home key is the resolution.

notes.text: Sonata form: the {{c1::exposition}} presents the themes in the home and a contrasting key, the {{c2::development}} fragments and modulates, the {{c3::recapitulation}} brings both themes back in the home key.
The Classical symphony's four movements: a fast {{c1::sonata-form}} first movement, a {{c2::slow}} lyrical second, a {{c3::minuet (later scherzo)}} third, and a fast finale (rondo or sonata form).

notes.front: Why is Haydn called the father of the symphony and the string quartet?
notes.back: Across 104 symphonies and 68 quartets he fixed the four-movement plan, made motivic development the engine, and gave four instruments equal conversational roles, with wit.
notes.extra: Anchors: 'Surprise' Symphony No. 94, the 'London' symphonies, Op. 76 quartets.

notes.front: Why was the string quartet the ideal Classical genre?
notes.back: Two violins, viola and cello: four equal voices with one blended colour, so attention falls entirely on argument and form. Goethe: 'four rational people conversing'.

notes.front: What did Mozart perfect?
notes.back: Italian lyricism fused with German craft; opera as psychological ensemble; the piano concerto as dialogue between soloist and orchestra.
notes.extra: Anchors: Figaro, Don Giovanni; piano concertos Nos. 20 and 21; the 'Jupiter' Symphony; the Requiem.

notes.front: What was new about Mozart's operas?
notes.back: Ensembles in which several characters sing different feelings at once; music that characterises class and psychology; comedy and tragedy in one piece (Don Giovanni, a dramma giocoso).

notes.front: Opera seria vs opera buffa?
notes.back: Seria: mythic heroes, castrati, showpiece da capo arias, static. Buffa: comic everyday characters, fast ensembles, chain finales. Buffa's realism won (Figaro).

notes.front: What did Gluck's opera reform (1760s) demand?
notes.back: 'Beautiful simplicity': music serving the drama, no vocal display for its own sake, chorus and orchestra integrated. The line runs Gluck → Mozart → Wagner.

notes.front: What is an Alberti bass?
notes.back: A broken-chord accompaniment pattern (low–high–middle–high) that keeps a Classical keyboard texture moving under a melody; an instant period signature.
notes.extra: Hear it: Opening of Mozart's Sonata in C, K. 545.

notes.front: Beethoven's three periods: how do they differ?
notes.back: Early: Haydn and Mozart inherited (Symphonies 1–2, Op. 18). Middle 'heroic': Eroica, Fifth, Fidelio, Appassionata. Late: introspective, fugal, radical (Ninth, late quartets, Hammerklavier).

notes.front: Why is the Eroica (1804) a turning point?
notes.back: Twice the length of any symphony before it, driven by motivic development, with a funeral march. The symphony became a statement about humanity, not an evening's entertainment.

notes.front: What does Beethoven's Fifth demonstrate about motivic development?
notes.back: A whole movement grown from one four-note cell (short-short-short-LONG), which then haunts the later movements; minor turning to major as a narrative of struggle to triumph.
notes.analogy: A novel written from a single sentence, re-angled on every page.

notes.front: What did the Ninth Symphony (1824) do that changed the genre?
notes.back: Brought voices and a text (Schiller's 'Ode to Joy') into the symphony, making it a moral and philosophical message. Template for Mahler and the Romantic 'giant' symphony.

notes.front: How did Beethoven change the composer's social position?
notes.back: From liveried court servant (Haydn) to independent artist living on publishers, subscriptions and an annuity on his own terms. The Romantic cult of the artist-genius starts here.

notes.front: Minuet vs scherzo?
notes.back: Minuet: elegant triple-time courtly dance, moderate, ABA with trio. Scherzo ('joke', Beethoven): same slot and triple metre but fast, driving, often humorous or menacing.

notes.front: What can you hear that says 'Romantic'?
notes.back: A big colourful orchestra, rich chromatic harmony, rubato and extreme dynamics, long lyrical melodies, descriptive titles, and extremes of scale from two-minute piano pieces to four-hour operas.

notes.front: What did Romanticism value that Classicism did not?
notes.back: Individual feeling over balance, the sublime and infinite, nature, the supernatural, folk and nation, the artist as genius. Music was ranked the highest art because it was wordless.
notes.extra: Thinkers: E. T. A. Hoffmann on Beethoven; Schopenhauer: music expresses the will itself.

notes.front: Programme music vs absolute music?
notes.back: Programme: instrumental music depicting a story, scene or idea (Berlioz, Liszt, Strauss). Absolute: music about nothing but itself (Brahms, defended by Hanslick). The 'War of the Romantics'.

notes.front: What was new in Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique (1830)?
notes.back: An autobiographical programme; an idée fixe (the beloved's theme) transformed across all five movements; orchestration itself as expression (muted strings, E♭ clarinet grotesque, bells).

notes.front: Idée fixe, thematic transformation and leitmotif: how do they differ?
notes.back: Idée fixe (Berlioz): one recurring theme. Thematic transformation (Liszt): a theme's character changed to generate a whole piece. Leitmotif (Wagner): a web of short motifs for characters and ideas, combined and developed.

notes.front: What is a symphonic poem?
notes.back: A single-movement orchestral work whose form follows a literary or pictorial idea rather than sonata convention. Liszt's Les Préludes, Smetana's Vltava, Strauss's Don Juan.

notes.front: What is the Lied, and why is Schubert its anchor?
notes.back: German art song for voice and piano in which the piano paints the poem (a spinning wheel, galloping hooves). Schubert wrote 600+ and invented the song cycle (Winterreise).
notes.analogy: A two-actor play: the singer says the words, the piano shows what is left unsaid.
notes.extra: Hear it: Erlkönig: one singer, four characters, relentless octave triplets as the horse.

notes.front: Why did the piano become the Romantic instrument?
notes.back: Iron frame gave power and sustain; the bourgeois home had one; one player could be an orchestra. It served both the intimate miniature (Chopin) and the public showpiece (Liszt).

notes.front: What do you listen for in Chopin?
notes.back: Piano only; bel canto melody over a wide-spaced bass, rubato, chromatic ornament, and Polish dances (mazurka, polonaise) as a national voice in exile. Nocturnes, ballades, études.

notes.front: Why did the virtuoso cult (Paganini, Liszt) arise in the 1830s–40s?
notes.back: Public concert halls and a ticket-buying middle class turned performance into spectacle. Liszt invented the solo recital, played from memory and turned the piano sideways to be seen.
notes.extra: 'Lisztomania' was Heine's word; fans fought over his gloves.

notes.front: What did Mendelssohn's 1829 Bach revival start?
notes.back: The concert hall as a museum of past masterworks. From here on, audiences mostly hear old music, and composers write against a canon.
notes.analogy: A gallery that stops buying new paintings and hangs the old masters instead.

notes.front: How do you hear musical nationalism, and why did it arise?
notes.back: Folk tunes and dance rhythms, modal colour, national legends and language. It grew with 19th-century nation-building and resistance to German-Italian dominance: Russia, Bohemia, Norway, later Finland and Hungary.
notes.extra: Anchors: Mussorgsky, Smetana's Má vlast, Dvořák, Grieg, Sibelius.

notes.front: Why does Mussorgsky matter beyond Russia?
notes.back: He rejected conservatory polish for speech-rhythm melody and raw modal harmony (Boris Godunov, Pictures at an Exhibition); Debussy heard a way out of German harmony.

notes.front: Brahms vs Wagner: the central divide of the century?
notes.back: Brahms: absolute music, Classical forms, Beethoven's heir, 'developing variation'. Wagner: music drama, myth, continuous melody, chromatic harmony, the total artwork.
notes.extra: Twist: Schoenberg called Brahms 'the progressive' and descended from both.

notes.front: What did Wagner's music drama reject, and what did it put in its place?
notes.back: Number opera with separate arias and applause. Instead: continuous music, myth, a hidden orchestra narrating psychology through leitmotifs, the Gesamtkunstwerk uniting all arts. The Ring, Tristan.

notes.front: Why is the Tristan chord (1859) a landmark?
notes.back: The opera opens with a dissonance that resolves only into another dissonance, and full resolution is withheld for four hours. Tonality stretched to its limit; the road to Schoenberg.
notes.analogy: A sentence whose clauses keep postponing the verb for four hours.

notes.front: What is chromaticism, and why did it erode tonality?
notes.back: Using notes outside the key, so chords slide by semitone and borrow from everywhere. The more they do, the less any home key is felt; by late Wagner, Liszt and Mahler the centre barely holds.
notes.analogy: Add enough exceptions to a rule and nobody can say what the rule is.

notes.front: If chromaticism weakens the tonal key plot, what did late Romantic composers use to hold a long work together?
notes.back: Other glue: a programme or story (Berlioz, Liszt), recurring motifs (Wagner's leitmotifs, Liszt's thematic transformation) and sheer orchestral colour. Sonata-style key drama alone no longer carried the form.

notes.front: Verdi vs Wagner: the Italian and German operatic ideals?
notes.back: Verdi: voice first, hummable melody, human and political drama (Rigoletto, La traviata, Aida, Otello). Wagner: orchestra first, myth, continuous flow.
notes.extra: Politics: 'Va, pensiero' from Nabucco became an anthem of Italian unification.

notes.front: What is verismo?
notes.back: Late Italian operatic realism: ordinary people, raw emotion, lush orchestration (Puccini's La bohème, Tosca; Mascagni). Puccini is a direct ancestor of Hollywood scoring.

notes.front: Why did the orchestra grow so large in the 19th century?
notes.back: Valve brass, bigger halls and audiences, and an appetite for colour and power. Berlioz's orchestration treatise, Wagner's covered pit and tubas, Mahler's hundred-plus players.

notes.front: What does Tchaikovsky anchor?
notes.back: Ballet as symphonic music (Swan Lake, Nutcracker) and the confessional, melody-driven symphony (Nos. 4–6). Russian but cosmopolitan, unlike the nationalist 'Mighty Handful'.

notes.front: What is rubato, and which era does it signal?
notes.back: Expressive stretching and compressing of tempo ('robbed time'). A Romantic signature, the opposite of Baroque motor rhythm.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: Why is Mahler the bridge from Romanticism to modernism?
notes.back: The symphony as a whole world: nature, death, irony, folk marches beside the sublime, songs inside symphonies, enormous forces and length. Schoenberg's generation idolised him.
notes.extra: Anchors: Symphonies 1, 2 'Resurrection', 5, 9; Das Lied von der Erde.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: What does Richard Strauss show about the end of Romanticism?
notes.back: He pushed tone poems (Don Juan) and operas (Salome, Elektra) to the edge of atonality, then stepped back to a sweetened style (Der Rosenkavalier). Modernism was a choice, not a destiny.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: How do you hear Debussy as a break with German Romanticism?
notes.back: Chords as colour rather than steps in a progression, whole-tone and pentatonic scales, parallel chords, blurred rhythm, timbre at the centre. Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune (1894), La Mer.
notes.analogy: Harmony as paint rather than grammar: chords chosen for colour, not for what they imply next.
notes.extra: Influences: Javanese gamelan at the 1889 Paris Exposition, Russian modal music, Symbolist poetry. He disliked the label 'Impressionist'.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: Why does the whole-tone scale sound as it does?
notes.back: Six equal whole steps: no perfect fifth, no leading tone, so nothing points anywhere. Floating and directionless; Debussy's Voiles, dream sequences in film.
notes.analogy: A round room: nowhere for the ear to find a corner and rest.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: Ravel vs Debussy?
notes.back: Ravel: precise, Classical forms, dazzling orchestration, clockwork rhythm (Boléro, Daphnis). Debussy: fluid form, blurred edges, suggestion. Both French, both colourists, often confused.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: What did Stravinsky's Rite of Spring (1913) do to rhythm?
notes.back: Made rhythm the primary force: irregular shifting metres, unpredictable accents on repeated chords, ostinato blocks, polytonal stacks, primitive orchestration. Hence the riot.
notes.extra: Hear it: 'Augurs of Spring': one dissonant chord hammered in a steady pulse with accents that refuse to settle.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: Stravinsky's three periods?
notes.back: Russian (Firebird, Petrushka, Rite); neoclassical (Pulcinella, Symphony of Psalms: old forms with wrong notes); serial (late, after Schoenberg's death).
notes.analogy: A chameleon who kept his own skeleton: the dry rhythm and clear blocks never change.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: What did neoclassicism (1920s) react against?
notes.back: Romantic grandeur and expressionist angst after WWI. Instead: small ensembles, Baroque and Classical forms, clarity, irony, objectivity (Stravinsky, Prokofiev's 'Classical' Symphony, Hindemith, Les Six).

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: Why did Schoenberg abandon tonality around 1908?
notes.back: Chromaticism had already dissolved the key centre; he drew the conclusion: 'emancipation of the dissonance', chords no longer needing to resolve. Erwartung, Pierrot lunaire.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: What is musical expressionism?
notes.back: Inner anguish made audible: extreme intervals, no tonic, violent contrasts, Sprechstimme (half-spoken singing). Pierrot lunaire, Berg's Wozzeck.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: What problem did the twelve-tone method (1921) solve, and how?
notes.back: Free atonality had no way to build large forms. Order all 12 pitches into a row and derive everything from it, each pitch returning only after all 12 have sounded: no tonic can form.
notes.analogy: A constitution for a republic with no king: every note gets an equal turn.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: Name the transformations of a twelve-tone row and what each does to its intervals. How many forms result?
notes.back: Prime (original); retrograde (played backwards); inversion (every interval flipped upside down); retrograde inversion. Each can start on any of 12 pitches: 4 × 12 = 48 forms.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: Why does twelve-tone music sound 'tuneless' to most listeners?
notes.back: Listening relies on tonal hierarchy to predict what comes next; with no home pitch, wide leaps and constant change, prediction fails and memory cannot chunk the phrases.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: Berg vs Webern: the two pupils?
notes.back: Berg: lyrical, hides tonal chords and Romantic warmth inside the system (Violin Concerto, Wozzeck, Lulu). Webern: aphoristic, crystalline, pointillistic; the model for post-1945 serialists.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: How did Bartók make a modernism out of folk music?
notes.back: Fieldwork recording peasant songs gave him asymmetric rhythms, modes and pentatonics, which he fused with percussive dissonance and tight forms. A third path beside Schoenberg and Stravinsky.
notes.extra: Anchors: Six string quartets, Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta, Concerto for Orchestra; 'night music' slow movements.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: Stravinsky vs Schoenberg: the modernist fork?
notes.back: Stravinsky: rhythm, objectivity, tonal-ish blocks, masks and irony. Schoenberg: pitch organisation, inner expression, the German tradition continued by other means. Both rejected Romantic sentiment.

notes.deck: Music History::08 Late Romantic to Modernism
notes.front: What constraint shaped Shostakovich, and how do you hear it?
notes.back: Soviet 'socialist realism' demanded accessible heroic tonality (the 1936 Pravda attack). He answered with the Fifth: outwardly triumphant, inwardly ironic; grotesque marches, hollow victories.
notes.analogy: A loyal poem with a second meaning for those who know how to read it.
notes.extra: Signature: The DSCH motif (D–E♭–C–B) embedded as a personal cipher.

notes.front: Why did many post-1945 composers embrace total serialism?
notes.back: After the war, Romantic and nationalist culture seemed tainted; rational, objective systems felt clean. Boulez, Stockhausen and Babbitt serialised rhythm, dynamics and timbre too.

notes.front: What did Messiaen contribute?
notes.back: Birdsong transcribed, modes of limited transposition, non-retrogradable rhythms, Indian talas, Catholic mysticism in sound; teacher of Boulez, Stockhausen and Xenakis. Quartet for the End of Time.

notes.front: Musique concrète (Schaeffer, Paris 1948) vs elektronische Musik (Cologne, 1950s)?
notes.back: Concrète: real-world recorded sounds cut, looped and transformed on tape. Cologne (Stockhausen): sounds built from scratch with oscillators under serial control. They merged in Gesang der Jünglinge (1956).
notes.analogy: Photography versus painting: capturing found sounds versus constructing them from nothing.

notes.front: How does musique concrète's use of recorded sound differ from hip-hop sampling?
notes.back: Concrète transformed recorded sounds (cut, looped, reversed) into abstract new objects whose source is often unrecognisable. Hip-hop sampling keeps recognisable recordings and places them over a groove, so the source is part of the meaning.

notes.front: What did tape and electronics change about music in principle?
notes.back: No performer, no notation, no instrument needed: any sound is material and the work is the fixed recording. Listening without seeing a source ('acousmatic') became normal.

notes.front: What is the point of Cage's 4'33" (1952)?
notes.back: A frame of silence turns ambient sound into the piece: music is attention, not the composer's intention. Zen influence; chance operations (I Ching) removed the ego from composing.
notes.analogy: A picture frame hung on a blank wall: whatever appears inside it becomes the art.

notes.front: Serialism vs Cage's indeterminacy: opposite methods, same enemy?
notes.back: Both rejected Romantic self-expression: serialism by total control of every parameter, Cage by giving control away to chance. Boulez and Cage corresponded, then fell out.

notes.front: What did sound-mass composers (Ligeti, Penderecki, Xenakis) do?
notes.back: Replaced melody and harmony with texture: dense clusters of many canonic lines (Ligeti's micropolyphony, Atmosphères), glissandi and noise (Penderecki's Threnody), density and shape as the material.
notes.analogy: Painting with a spray can rather than a pencil: shapes and densities, not lines.
notes.extra: Hear it: Kubrick's 2001 and The Shining use Ligeti and Penderecki.

notes.front: What did minimalism (1960s: Young, Riley, Reich, Glass) react against, and how do you hear it?
notes.back: Against serialist complexity and academic inaccessibility. Steady pulse, consonant harmony, repetition, slow audible change, long duration; roots in jazz, gamelan, African drumming, Indian music.
notes.analogy: A tide: pattern changing so slowly you notice only in retrospect.

notes.front: What is Reich's phasing, and what is 'music as a gradual process'?
notes.back: Two identical loops drift slowly out of sync, creating new patterns nobody wrote (It's Gonna Rain, Piano Phase). The process is audible and is the piece. Music for 18 Musicians.
notes.analogy: Two windscreen wipers slightly out of time: watch them drift apart and realign.

notes.front: How does Reich's phasing differ from a Baroque ground bass, though both repeat?
notes.back: A ground bass repeats a bass pattern while the composer varies the parts above it. In phasing the loops stay unchanged and only their alignment shifts, so new patterns emerge from the process itself.

notes.front: Glass vs Reich?
notes.back: Glass: additive rhythm, arpeggiated chord cycles, opera and film (Einstein on the Beach, Koyaanisqatsi). Reich: phasing, canons, speech melody, African and gamelan rhythm, percussion ensembles.

notes.front: What is spectralism (Grisey, Murail, 1970s)?
notes.back: Composing from the measured overtone spectrum of real sounds: a chord that is literally the harmonics of a trombone note. Harmony and timbre become one thing; the overtone series returns as subject.

notes.front: What is 'holy minimalism' (Pärt, Górecki, Tavener)?
notes.back: 1970s onward: slow, spare, triadic, sacred music of stillness; Pärt's tintinnabuli method (Spiegel im Spiegel, Fratres). A deliberate exit from avant-garde complexity.

notes.front: Where does film music come from stylistically?
notes.back: Late-Romantic opera: Korngold and Steiner (Viennese émigrés) brought Wagnerian leitmotif and the big orchestra to Hollywood; John Williams revived it (Star Wars). Herrmann added modernist edge.

notes.front: Why did 'classical' music lose its central cultural place in the 20th century?
notes.back: Recording and popular music took the audience; the avant-garde alienated listeners; the concert hall became a museum of 1700–1900 repertoire. Film, minimalism and crossover partly reconnected.

notes.front: Where did the blues come from, and what are its hearable marks?
notes.back: African-American work songs, field hollers and spirituals in the post-slavery Deep South. Blue notes (bent thirds and sevenths), call and response, AAB verses, a 12-bar chord cycle, directness.

notes.front: Write out the 12-bar blues chord pattern bar by bar, in Roman numerals.
notes.back: Bars 1–4: I. Bars 5–6: IV. Bars 7–8: I. Bar 9: V. Bar 10: IV. Bars 11–12: I (the last bar often a V turnaround).

notes.front: Why does the 12-bar blues use the chords I, IV and V in this order?
notes.back: They are tonic, subdominant and dominant: rest, departure and tension. The pattern compresses home, departure, tension and return into twelve bars, so each chorus feels like a complete cycle.

notes.front: What is a blue note?
notes.back: A pitch bent between major and minor (the third, fifth or seventh), from African pitch practice meeting European harmony. Guitars, voices and horns can do it; the piano fakes it with both notes.
notes.analogy: Singing between the piano's keys.

notes.front: Ragtime (Joplin) vs early jazz?
notes.back: Ragtime is composed and notated piano music: syncopated right hand over a steady march-like left hand, no improvisation, no swing. A precursor, not yet jazz.

notes.front: Why was jazz born in New Orleans (c. 1900–20), and from what?
notes.back: A port mixing Black blues, Creole European training, brass-band tradition (cheap post-Civil-War instruments), ragtime and Caribbean rhythm. Collective improvisation; Louis Armstrong then made it a soloist's art.
notes.extra: Anchor: Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings (1925–28): 'West End Blues'.

notes.front: What is jazz improvisation actually based on?
notes.back: Spontaneous melody over a fixed cycle of chords ('the changes') and form of a tune: play the head, take solos over repeated choruses, play the head again.
notes.analogy: Agreed floor plan, improvised furniture: everyone knows where the walls are.

notes.front: What is swing feel?
notes.back: Beats divided unevenly (long–short, roughly triplet-based eighths) with a forward lean and lift from the rhythm section. The rhythmic DNA that separates jazz from classical and from straight rock.
notes.analogy: A walk with a lilt rather than a march: long-short, long-short, leaning forward.

notes.front: What defined the Swing Era (c. 1935–45), and why does Ellington stand apart?
notes.back: Big bands (brass, reeds, rhythm) playing arranged riffs with call and response between sections: America's dance-pop. Ellington composed for his players' individual sounds (Mood Indigo, Ko-Ko).
notes.extra: Others: Count Basie (riff-based, Kansas City), Benny Goodman (the crossover 'King of Swing').

notes.front: Bebop (Parker, Gillespie, c. 1945): what did it react against, and how does it sound?
notes.back: Against commercial dance swing. Fast tempos, dense chromatic harmony, angular virtuoso lines, small combos, music for listening not dancing. Parker's 'Ko-Ko', 'Salt Peanuts'.

notes.front: What did bebop do with harmony?
notes.back: Extended chords (9ths, 11ths, 13ths), altered notes, tritone substitutions, rapid ii–V–I chains, chord substitutions on standard tunes ('rhythm changes', later Coltrane's 'Giant Steps').

notes.front: Why is ii–V–I the core jazz progression?
notes.back: Subdominant, dominant, tonic in one compact unit; chains of them move smoothly through keys, and most standards are built from them.

notes.text: The 32-bar {{c1::AABA}} song form of Tin Pan Alley standards ('I Got Rhythm', 'Over the Rainbow'): the A section 8 bars, repeated, a contrasting 8-bar {{c2::bridge}}, then A again; one pass is a {{c3::chorus}}.

notes.front: Cool jazz vs hard bop (1950s)?
notes.back: Cool: relaxed, light tone, arranged, classical touches, West Coast (Miles's Birth of the Cool, Brubeck, MJQ). Hard bop: East Coast reaction, blues and gospel-rooted, driving, funky (Blakey, Horace Silver).

notes.front: Modal jazz (Kind of Blue, 1959): what problem did it solve?
notes.back: Bebop's dense changes left soloists running scales. Staying on one mode for 8 or 16 bars ('So What': D Dorian) freed them to think melodically and in space. Coltrane took it to A Love Supreme.
notes.analogy: Taking the fences down so the horse can run.

notes.front: How does a soloist's approach differ between a bebop ii–V–I chain and a modal piece like 'So What'?
notes.back: Bebop: the harmony changes every bar or two, so the soloist outlines each chord's notes and connects them. Modal: one scale (D Dorian) lasts 16 bars, so the soloist shapes melody, space and rhythm freely.

notes.front: What did free jazz (Ornette Coleman, Cecil Taylor, late Coltrane) abandon?
notes.back: Fixed chord changes, often metre and tonality; collective improvisation returned. Tied to 1960s Black liberation energy. Coleman's Free Jazz (1960), Coltrane's Ascension.

notes.front: What was fusion (c. 1970)?
notes.back: Jazz improvisation over rock and funk grooves with electric instruments and studio editing: Miles's Bitches Brew, Weather Report, Herbie Hancock's Head Hunters.

notes.front: Swing vs bebop vs modal: three quick tells?
notes.back: Swing: big band, arranged sections, dance tempo, riffs. Bebop: small group, frantic tempo, chord-dense solos. Modal: spacious, few chords, long melodic solos.

notes.front: How did blues become rock'n'roll (mid-1950s)?
notes.back: Electrified urban blues (Chicago: Muddy Waters) + jump-blues R&B + country/hillbilly + a boogie backbeat, sold to teenagers by radio and the 45. Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Elvis as crossover.
notes.extra: Hear it: Chuck Berry's songs are 12-bar blues at a faster tempo with guitar intros.

notes.front: What is the backbeat, and why does it matter?
notes.back: A snare accent on beats 2 and 4 of a 4/4 bar. It is the physical pulse that distinguishes rock and R&B from swing's even four and the march's 1–3.
notes.analogy: The clap-along beat: an audience claps on 2 and 4, not on 1 and 3.

notes.front: What did gospel give to soul and R&B?
notes.back: Vocal style (melisma, shouts, ad libs), call and response, handclaps and chord progressions. Ray Charles secularised gospel songs ('I Got a Woman'); Aretha and Otis followed.

notes.front: Motown vs Stax?
notes.back: Motown (Detroit): polished pop crossover, strings, tambourine, the Funk Brothers' hit factory. Stax (Memphis): raw Southern soul, horns, gospel grit (Otis Redding, Sam & Dave).

notes.front: What did James Brown change about the beat (c. 1965–70)?
notes.back: Everything hits 'The One', then syncopated interlocking riffs on guitar, bass, horns and drums; harmony static on one chord; every instrument plays like a drum. Rhythm over melody.
notes.extra: Lineage: West African polyrhythm reborn; the raw material hip-hop would later sample.

notes.front: What was the Beatles' significance beyond fame?
notes.back: From beat-group to studio art in four years: the album as a unit (Revolver, Sgt. Pepper), tape tricks, Indian, classical and avant-garde borrowings, self-written songs. Pop became art.

notes.front: Why does rock harmony favour the ♭VII chord and power chords?
notes.back: Blues and Mixolydian roots make the flat seventh natural; a power chord (root + fifth, no third) stays clear under distortion because few partials clash.

notes.front: What was progressive rock, and what did it provoke?
notes.back: Long forms, concept albums, classical and jazz borrowings, synthesisers, virtuosity (Pink Floyd, Yes, King Crimson). Its grandeur was punk's target.

notes.front: What did punk (1976–77) react against, and what did it leave behind?
notes.back: Against prog and arena bloat, virtuosity and polish: three chords, two minutes, do-it-yourself. Legacy: post-punk, indie, hardcore, grunge and the idea that anyone can start a band.

notes.front: How did heavy metal grow out of blues-rock?
notes.back: Cream, Hendrix and Led Zeppelin's amplified blues → Black Sabbath's slow tritone riffs → Judas Priest and speed. Riff-based, distorted, modal (Aeolian, Phrygian), power as aesthetic.

notes.front: What defines reggae, and what did dub start?
notes.back: Offbeat guitar 'skank', bass-led 'one drop' drums, slow tempo (Marley). Dub (King Tubby, Lee Perry): remixing the multitrack with echo and dropouts, the birth of the producer as artist and of the remix.

notes.front: How was hip-hop born (Bronx, 1973–79)?
notes.back: DJ Kool Herc isolated and looped the drum 'break' of funk records on two turntables; MCs rhymed over it; breakdancing and graffiti alongside. 'Rapper's Delight' (1979) took it to vinyl.
notes.analogy: The break was the best ten seconds of the record, so the DJ made it last ten minutes.

notes.front: What did sampling do to the idea of composition, and what stopped its golden age?
notes.back: Music made from pieces of other records, recontextualised (Public Enemy, De La Soul, 1986–93). Copyright rulings (1991) made dense collage unaffordable; production shifted to drum machines and cleared loops.

notes.front: Disco → house → techno: what is the lineage?
notes.back: Disco (1970s, four-on-the-floor, DJ-extended mixes) → Chicago house (1980s, drum machines, Frankie Knuckles) → Detroit techno (Atkins, May: futurism via Kraftwerk) → rave and EDM.

notes.front: What is four-on-the-floor?
notes.back: A kick drum on every beat of 4/4: the constant physical floor of disco, house and techno.

notes.front: What was Kraftwerk's role?
notes.back: The first fully electronic pop (Autobahn 1974, Trans-Europe Express): machine rhythm and synth melodies. Sampled in early hip-hop ('Planet Rock') and the acknowledged source of techno.

notes.front: Why did 'failed' machines like the Roland TR-808 and TB-303 define genres?
notes.back: Their unrealistic sounds (boomy 808 kick, squelchy 303 bass) flopped with pros, so they were cheap second-hand for Black producers in Chicago, Detroit and New York: electro, hip-hop, acid house.

notes.front: Where does country music come from?
notes.back: Appalachian ballads of British origin plus blues, gospel and the fiddle; recorded from the 1920s (Carter Family, Jimmie Rodgers), industrialised in Nashville. It feeds rockabilly and rock'n'roll.

notes.text: In 1960s pop form, the section whose words change each time and advance the story is the {{c1::verse}}; the section that repeats the hook and title is the {{c2::chorus}}; the contrasting section before the final repeats is the {{c3::bridge}}.

notes.front: What is a raga?
notes.back: Far more than a scale: a melodic framework with set ascending and descending patterns, characteristic phrases, emphasised notes, a mood (rasa) and a traditional time of day. The basis for improvisation.
notes.analogy: A character rather than an alphabet: you can improvise its speech because you know how it behaves.

notes.front: What is a tala?
notes.back: A cyclic rhythmic frame of a fixed number of beats with internal groupings (tintal: 16 as 4+4+4+4). The first beat, sam, is the point of return where soloist and drummer converge.
notes.analogy: A circular running track with one marked line: take any route, but land on the line.
notes.extra: Hear it: Audiences count claps and waves on their hands and applaud when a long improvisation lands exactly on sam.

notes.front: How does a Hindustani performance unfold?
notes.back: A drone (tanpura) fixes the tonic; alap explores the raga slowly without pulse; the tabla enters with a composition (gat) and the music accelerates to a climax.

notes.front: How does tension and release work in a raga performance compared with Western tonality?
notes.back: Western: tension comes from leaving the tonic through harmony and resolving by cadence. Raga: the tonic drone never changes, so tension comes from melodic emphasis and rhythmic build-up, resolving at the tala's first beat (sam).

notes.front: Why does Indian classical music have no harmony?
notes.back: Complexity went into pitch and rhythm instead: a single drone tonic, microtonal ornaments (meend, gamak) and 22 shruti, plus intricate talas. Chord changes would destroy the drone-centred depth.

notes.front: Hindustani vs Carnatic?
notes.back: North: Persian and Mughal influence, sitar, sarod, tabla, long slow alap. South: Hindu temple tradition, composed kritis (Tyagaraja), violin and mridangam, the 72-scale melakarta system, vocal percussion.

notes.front: What is a gamelan, and how is its music built?
notes.back: A Javanese or Balinese ensemble of tuned bronze metallophones, gongs and drums. Stratified polyphony: a core melody in the middle, slow gongs marking the cycle, fast elaborating parts above; drums lead, no conductor.
notes.analogy: The layers of a clock: gongs as the hour hand, core melody as the minute hand, elaboration as the second hand.

notes.front: Why does gamelan sound 'out of tune' to Western ears?
notes.back: Two tuning systems, slendro (five roughly equal steps) and pelog (seven unequal), with no standard: each ensemble is tuned to itself, and paired instruments are deliberately detuned for shimmer (ombak).

notes.front: Why can't you play gamelan music simply by retuning it to a piano's equal temperament?
notes.back: Slendro and pelog intervals differ from Western semitones, and each ensemble is built and tuned as a unit, with paired instruments deliberately detuned for shimmer. Equal temperament would erase the characteristic intervals and the shimmer.

notes.front: Balinese vs Javanese gamelan?
notes.back: Bali: fast, bright, dramatic, interlocking kotekan where two players share one rapid line. Java (court): slow, refined, meditative, soft-voiced singing.

notes.front: How did gamelan influence Western composers?
notes.back: Debussy heard it in 1889 and loosened harmony toward colour; Britten, Lou Harrison and Reich took its cyclic layering and interlocking parts into minimalism.

notes.front: What is going on in West African polyrhythm?
notes.back: Several interlocking patterns with different groupings (3 against 2, 4 against 3) locked to a repeating bell timeline; a master drummer signals changes; no single downbeat, the listener chooses a perspective.

notes.front: In a 3-against-2 polyrhythm, how long until the two patterns realign, and where do they coincide?
notes.back: They realign after 6 pulses (the least common multiple of 3 and 2) and coincide only on the first pulse of the cycle. In between, the listener hears the tension of two grids.

notes.front: What does the standard 12-pulse bell pattern do for the ensemble?
notes.back: Its asymmetric seven strokes (x.x.xx.x.x.x) fix where the cycle starts, so players hearing different groupings of the same twelve pulses stay aligned.
notes.analogy: A clock face everyone can see while each person dances to a different count.

notes.front: How did West African rhythm shape the music of the Americas?
notes.back: Through the slave trade: Cuban clave and son, Brazilian samba, swing, funk's layered riffs, hip-hop's loops, and offbeat phrasing everywhere. Also the ethos of participatory, cyclic, call-and-response music.

notes.front: Why is call and response everywhere in African-American music?
notes.back: A leader–group alternation that structures participation: sermons, work songs, blues, gospel, swing-band section riffs, hip-hop crowd chants. African in origin, now global.

notes.front: Cyclic vs linear musical time?
notes.back: Gamelan, tala and African timelines organise music around repeating cycles that you enter and leave; Western classical music since 1600 tells a goal-directed harmonic story with a beginning and an end.
notes.extra: Convergence: Minimalism and dance music are Western returns to cyclic time.

notes.front: What is a maqam, and why can't a piano play one?
notes.back: The melodic mode system of Arabic, Turkish and Persian music: scale, characteristic phrases and mood, like raga. Many use intervals between the Western semitones (roughly quarter tones).
